section.title: The Fall of Jericho
section.sectionRationale: The first city of the conquest falls, and it falls in the strangest possible way. God's battle plan is not a siege but a procession: march around the walls behind the ark, blow the horns, keep silent, and on the seventh day shout. The wall collapses, the city is devoted to the LORD, and only Rahab and her household are spared. It is one movement, the fall of Jericho, which teaches from the outset that the land is the LORD's gift, taken by faith and obedience, not by military might.
section.thesis: God gives Jericho to Israel before a blow is struck, so the bizarre, unwarlike strategy strips away every ground for boasting and makes the victory unmistakably His; the walls fall by faith, the guilty city comes under judgment, and the believing outsider is saved.
section.frameNote: Four beats: God's promise and the strange battle plan, verses 1 to 5; the six days of silent marching, verses 6 to 14; the seventh day, the shout, and the fall of the wall, verses 15 to 21; and Rahab spared while the city is burned, with Joshua's curse, verses 22 to 27.

units.label: The promise and the strange battle plan
units.note: I have delivered Jericho into your hand

verses.text: Now Jericho was tightly shut up because of the Israelites. No one went out and no one came in.
And the LORD said to Joshua, “Behold, I have delivered Jericho into your hand, along with its king and its mighty men of valor.
March around the city with all the men of war, circling the city one time. Do this for six days.
Have seven priests carry seven rams’ horns in front of the ark. Then on the seventh day, march around the city seven times, while the priests blow the horns.

And when there is a long blast of the ram’s horn and you hear its sound, have all the people give a mighty shout. Then the wall of the city will collapse and all your people will charge straight into the city.”

units.label: Six days of silent marching
units.note: do not let one word come out of your mouth until I tell you

verses.text: So Joshua son of Nun summoned the priests and said, “Take up the ark of the covenant and have seven priests carry seven rams’ horns in front of the ark of the LORD.”
And he told the people, “Advance and march around the city, with the armed troops going ahead of the ark of the LORD.”
After Joshua had spoken to the people, seven priests carrying seven rams’ horns before the LORD advanced and blew the horns, and the ark of the covenant of the LORD followed them.
While the horns continued to sound, the armed troops marched ahead of the priests who blew the horns, and the rear guard followed the ark.
But Joshua had commanded the people: “Do not give a battle cry or let your voice be heard; do not let one word come out of your mouth until the day I tell you to shout. Then you are to shout!”
So he had the ark of the LORD carried around the city, circling it once. And the people returned to the camp and spent the night there.
Joshua got up early the next morning, and the priests took the ark of the LORD.

And the seven priests carrying seven rams’ horns kept marching ahead of the ark of the LORD and blowing the horns. The armed troops went in front of them and the rear guard followed the ark of the LORD, while the horns kept sounding.
So on the second day they marched around the city once and returned to the camp. They did this for six days.

units.label: The seventh day and the fall of the wall
units.note: shout, for the LORD has given you the city

verses.text: Then on the seventh day, they got up at dawn and marched around the city seven times in the same manner. That was the only day they circled the city seven times.
After the seventh time around, the priests blew the horns, and Joshua commanded the people, “Shout! For the LORD has given you the city!
Now the city and everything in it must be {{cherem|devoted to the LORD for destruction}}. Only Rahab the prostitute and all those with her in her house will live, because she hid the spies we sent.

But keep away from the things devoted to destruction, lest you yourself be set apart for destruction. If you take any of these, you will set apart the camp of Israel for destruction and bring disaster upon it.
For all the silver and gold and all the articles of bronze and iron are {{qodesh|holy}} to the LORD; they must go into His treasury.”

So when the rams’ horns sounded, the people shouted. When they heard the blast of the horn, the people gave a great {{teruah|shout}}, and the wall collapsed. Then all the people charged straight into the city and captured it.
With the edge of the sword they devoted to destruction everything in the city, man and woman, young and old, oxen, sheep, and donkeys.

units.label: Rahab spared and the city burned
units.note: she has lived among the Israelites to this day

verses.text: Meanwhile, Joshua told the two men who had spied out the land, “Go into the house of the prostitute and bring out the woman and all who are with her, just as you promised her.”
So the young spies went in and brought out Rahab, her father and mother and brothers, and all who belonged to her. They brought out her whole family and settled them outside the camp of Israel.
Then the Israelites burned up the city and everything in it. However, they put the silver and gold and articles of bronze and iron into the treasury of the LORD’s house.

And Joshua spared Rahab the prostitute, with her father’s household and all who belonged to her, because she hid the men Joshua had sent to spy out Jericho. So she has lived among the Israelites to this day.

At that time Joshua invoked this solemn oath: “Cursed before the LORD is the man who rises up and rebuilds this city, Jericho; at the cost of his firstborn he will lay its foundations; at the cost of his youngest he will set up its gates.”
So the LORD was with Joshua, and his fame spread throughout the land.

cherem.gloss: That which is devoted to the LORD irrevocably, set apart either for destruction or for His treasury. Jericho, the firstfruits of the land, is placed wholly under the cherem: its people fall under judgment, and its silver and gold go into the LORD's house. As firstfruits it belongs entirely to God; to seize any of it for oneself, as Achan will, is sacrilege that brings the ban upon the thief.

qodesh.gloss: Holiness, that which is set apart to God. The metals of Jericho are declared holy to the LORD and must enter His treasury, not private hands. Being holy, they are removed from ordinary use and reserved for God; the same holiness that consecrates makes it deadly to treat what is God's as common, tying this chapter to the disaster of chapter 7.

teruah.gloss: A loud shout, a blast, a war cry or cry of acclamation. On the seventh day the silent people finally give the great teruah, and the wall falls. The shout is not what topples the stone; it is the appointed act of faith and worship, a victory cry raised at God's word before the victory is seen, so that the fall is plainly God's doing in response to obedient faith.

basic.context: Jericho is sealed tight, but God tells Joshua the city is already given into his hand. Then comes the plan, and it is nothing like a siege. For six days the army is to march around the city once each day behind the ark, with priests blowing rams' horns, and the people utterly silent. On the seventh day they march around seven times, and at Joshua's word they shout, and the wall collapses. The city is devoted to the LORD, destroyed in judgment, its metals given to God's treasury, while Rahab and her family, who believed, are rescued. Joshua pronounces a curse on anyone who rebuilds it. The question at the heart of it all is: how is the promised land actually won?
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative, and the New Testament reads it through faith: by faith the walls of Jericho fell down, Hebrews 11:30. The strange strategy is the point, designed so no one could credit human might. The chapter also raises the hard question of the herem, the devotion of the city to destruction, which must be handled honestly as God's judgment on entrenched Canaanite sin, with mercy always open, as Rahab shows. We do not derive rules for warfare from this unique, God-commanded event.
basic.originalLanguages: The city is placed under the cherem, devoted wholly to the LORD, its people to destruction and its metals as things qodesh, holy, to God's treasury. And the wall falls only after the people raise the teruah, the great shout, an act of obedient faith at God's word.
basic.typology: The walls falling by faith, apart from human strength, picture the victories God gives His people by faith rather than by their own power. Rahab spared in the midst of judgment pictures the salvation of believers, and the marked house recalls the Passover. Jericho as firstfruits devoted to God points to the firstfruits belonging wholly to the LORD.
basic.christ: Hebrews holds up Jericho as a triumph of faith, and it points to the victory won not by our strength but by Christ. As judgment fell on the guilty city while the believing outsider was saved, so at the cross judgment and mercy meet, and all who take refuge in Christ, like Rahab, are rescued from the wrath to come. Rahab herself enters the line of Jesus.
basic.god: God is the giver of victory: the city is delivered before a blow is struck. He is holy and just, bringing long-delayed judgment on Canaan's sin, and merciful, sparing all who believe. He is worthy of exclusive devotion, so that the firstfruits of the land belong wholly to Him. And He is faithful, being with Joshua just as He promised.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 11 credits the fall of Jericho to faith. Genesis 15 explains that God waited for the sin of the Amorites to reach its full measure. 2 Corinthians 10 says our weapons are not of the flesh. And 1 Kings 16 records the fulfillment of Joshua's curse when Jericho was rebuilt.
basic.oneStory: The first city of the promised land falls by faith, not by force, showing that the inheritance is God's gift. Judgment falls on the guilty city while believing Rahab is saved, a pattern of the gospel. It is a decisive step in God giving Israel the land, and it points to the greater victory and the greater rescue won in Christ.

context.literary:
For six days the narrative refuses to move faster than the marching itself. The exact order of the procession, armed troops, seven horn blowing priests, the ark, the rear guard, is spelled out at length in verses 8 and 9, then repeated almost word for word in verse 13, and summarized again in verse 14, so the reader experiences something of the same repetitive discipline Israel had to endure: nothing changes, day after day, and the text will not let us skip ahead. Then, on the seventh day, the pace suddenly breaks. Seven circuits are compressed into a single verse, and verses 20 and 21 pile up short clauses one after another, the people shouted, the wall collapsed, the people charged, they captured the city, they devoted it to destruction, mimicking in the grammar itself how suddenly everything happens once the silence finally ends.

The chapter also closes a story left open in chapter 2. The spies had sworn an oath to Rahab, and verse 22 sends them back to her house with the very words just as you promised her, tying this scene to that earlier promise rather than letting it stand as a new decision. And the closing note, so the LORD was with Joshua, and his fame spread throughout the land, verse 27, deliberately answers the LORD's opening promise in verse 2 and sets up a bitter irony for the very next chapter, where that same divine favor is withdrawn the moment hidden sin enters the camp.
context.historical:
Ancient armies often carried a god's image or standard before them into battle for good fortune; Israel carries the ark instead, the throne of the LORD's own presence, so the procession around Jericho functions less like a siege than like a moving act of worship. The rams' horns, shofars, differ from the silver trumpets Numbers 10:1-10 assigns to ordinary calls to march and to battle, tying Jericho's fall to the horn blasts of sacred assembly rather than routine warfare. Seven priests, seven horns, seven days, seven circuits: the sevenfold pattern echoes other sevenfold rhythms in Israel's worship, such as the seven days of a priest's ordination, Leviticus 8:33, and marks this as consecrated action rather than ordinary tactics.

The herem itself was not an idea unique to Israel. Centuries later the Moabite king Mesha boasted on his own inscription of devoting an Israelite town to complete destruction for his god Chemosh, using the same category of the ban, which shows every nation in the region recognized this kind of total consecration in war. What sets Israel's practice apart is not the vocabulary but the reason: Deuteronomy ties the ban on Canaan to centuries of patiently withheld judgment on real wickedness, not to securing a rival god's favor, and it falls under the command of the one true LORD rather than a deity competing for territory.
context.canonical:
The fall of Jericho becomes a byword for victory by faith, celebrated in Hebrews 11:30, and Rahab's own rescue earns a second commendation two verses later as one who did not perish with those who were disobedient, Hebrews 11:31. James goes further, naming Rahab alongside Abraham himself as proof that faith without works is dead, since she was justified by what she did in hiding the messengers and sending them out another way, James 2:25, an unlikely pairing of the father of the faithful with a Canaanite prostitute that levels the ground at the foot of true faith.

The chapter also puts into practice a law given before Israel ever crossed the Jordan: Deuteronomy had already commanded that the cities of these nations be left with nothing that breathes, so Israel would not learn their detestable ways, Deuteronomy 20:16-18. Jericho is the first test of that command, and it stands as the firstfruits of the whole land, wholly devoted to God, a status that frames the tragedy of the very next chapter, where Achan seizes what belonged to the LORD alone. Even Joshua's closing curse echoes older covenant language; his oath that whoever rebuilds Jericho will lose sons in the foundation and the gate recalls the double edged promise given to Abraham, that God would curse those who cursed his line, Genesis 12:3, now turned against a city standing under judgment rather than blessing.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer wants a generation that has never fought a battle in Canaan to learn, before any other city falls, exactly how this land will be won. Every unusual element of the plan, marching instead of storming, silence instead of battle cries, a shout instead of a weapon, removes any possible claim that Israelite skill or courage took the city, so that the first victory becomes the interpretive key for the whole conquest: everything after Jericho is won the same way, by trust in God's word rather than by strength of arms.

The author is equally deliberate about Rahab. Placed at the center of Israel's first triumph over Canaan is a Canaanite who believed, spared while her whole city fell under judgment, and the text takes care to note that she still lived among Israel to this day, verse 25, meaning at the time of writing. That detail tells the first hearers something about who truly belongs to the covenant people: not ancestry but faith in the LORD, a lesson Israel would need again whenever an outsider like Ruth later joined it by the very same kind of trust.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The command for absolute silence during six days of marching describes a specific, one time test of obedience tied to a specific promise, not a devotional technique to be repeated whenever believers want a breakthrough; the point was trust in this word for this battle, not silence as a formula that guarantees results elsewhere. Likewise, the destruction of Jericho's population describes a particular act of divine judgment carried out through Israel at a fixed moment in redemptive history, and the New Testament never treats it as a model for how any nation, including Israel itself, should treat conquered peoples afterward. What does carry forward is the pattern underneath both: obedience that waits for God's timing rather than forcing an outcome, and mercy that reaches even a condemned city the moment someone inside it turns in faith, exactly what happens for Rahab and for every believer since.

debates.question: How can the devoting of Jericho to destruction, the herem, be squared with the goodness of God?

views.label: Righteous judgment on ripened wickedness, with mercy open to faith
views.case: Scripture frames the conquest as God's just judgment on centuries of Canaanite evil that He patiently delayed until it was complete, Genesis 15:16 and Deuteronomy 9:4-5; it is judgment, not ethnic cleansing, since Rahab and her household are saved the moment they believe, and Israel itself is warned it will face the same judgment if it copies Canaan's sins, showing the standard is sin, not race.

views.label: A unique, bounded episode that dramatizes final judgment
views.case: The herem was a limited command tied to a specific land and moment in redemptive history, not a template for war; it functions as a vivid, earthly picture of the reality of divine judgment on unrepentant sin, pointing forward to the last judgment, while the salvation of Rahab in the same event holds out the mercy available to all who turn to God.

debates.bearing: Held together honestly, both affirm that God's judgment on sin is real and just and that His mercy is genuinely open, which is precisely why the guilty city falls while the believing prostitute is saved; the cross is where that same judgment and mercy finally meet.

debates.question: Does Rahab's whole household being spared with her show a household principle of salvation, or is it simply the outworking of the spies' oath?

views.label: A household principle, one believer's faith shelters those under her roof
views.case: The oath sworn in Joshua 2:12-14, our lives for your lives, explicitly ties safety to remaining inside Rahab's house behind the scarlet cord, and her whole family is drawn out together, verse 23, echoing the Passover lamb whose blood protected everyone under one roof, Exodus 12:13, a pattern the New Testament repeats when a jailer's whole household is saved through his own faith, Acts 16:31.

views.label: A specific, limited term of a spy's oath, not a general rule
views.case: The rescue rests strictly on the terms the spies swore, tied to Rahab hiding them and marked by a visible sign in her window, Joshua 2:18-19; it is a legal promise fulfilled precisely as sworn, not a doctrine about how any household is saved, and nothing in the text turns it into a rule for others.

debates.bearing: The narrative itself only records a specific oath kept exactly as sworn, but the shape of it, one person's faith and the shelter given through it reaching a whole household, is the same shape Scripture returns to elsewhere; the safest reading holds the concrete promise to Rahab and the wider biblical pattern together without turning either into an automatic guarantee apart from personal faith.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond the three words already named, the chapter's very first line sets the tone with a wordplay: Jericho was tightly shut up, a phrase built in Hebrew by doubling the root sagar, to shut, back to back, an emphatic construction the language uses elsewhere to stress totality, much as Genesis 2:17 doubles the verb for dying to make you will surely die. The city is not merely closed; it is shutting and shut up, sealed against Israel as completely as language can say it, which makes the LORD's flat declaration in verse 2, I have delivered Jericho into your hand, land on the reader with full force, since no gate this firmly closed opens by ordinary means.

The horns the priests carry are shopharoth, ram's horns, the same shofar blown at Sinai, Exodus 19:16, and at the start of every jubilee year, Leviticus 25:9, an instrument tied throughout Israel's worship to the presence and voice of God rather than to ordinary battle signals; Numbers 10 gives Israel a separate pair of silver trumpets for gathering camp and sounding the charge, and pointedly does not use them here. Jericho falls to the sound of worship, not the sound of war.

At the center of the procession walks the aron, the ark, the throne of the LORD's own presence among His people, carried past by the very priests who sound the shofar, so the whole march is really a moving sanctuary circling a doomed city seven times before the sanctuary's God speaks the word that ends it.

The city itself is placed under cherem, devoted irrevocably to the LORD; its people fall under judgment while its silver, gold, bronze, and iron are called qodesh, holy, and set apart for the otsar, the treasury of the LORD's house, the same word used later for Solomon's temple storerooms, 1 Kings 7:51. And the wall falls only once the long silent people finally raise the teruah, the great shout, built on the same root behind the shout Israel raises for its first king, 1 Samuel 10:24, an appointed act of worship and acclamation rather than a noise loud enough on its own to shake stone. Shut, horn, ark, devoted, holy, treasury, shout: every word in the chapter turns an ordinary term of siege warfare into an act of worship, so that by the time the wall falls, the vocabulary itself has already declared whose victory this is.

typology.type: The walls falling by faith apart from human strength, Joshua 6:20
typology.fulfillment: For six days nothing about Israel's actions could topple a wall; marching in silence looks nothing like an assault, and the sole weapon on the seventh day is a shout. Hebrews credits the result entirely to faith, by faith the walls of Jericho fell down, after the people had marched around them for seven days, Hebrews 11:30, and Paul says believers wage their whole spiritual battle the same way, with weapons that are not of the flesh but carry divine power to demolish strongholds, 2 Corinthians 10:4. The type falls short only in scale: one wall came down at Jericho, but the strongholds Paul has in view are every proud thought raised against the knowledge of God, a far larger wall brought down the same way, by faith rather than force.

typology.type: Rahab saved in the midst of the city's judgment, Joshua 6:22-25
typology.fulfillment: Rahab's rescue is arranged before the battle even starts, sealed by an oath and a visible sign, the scarlet cord in her window, so that when judgment falls on the city she is already marked out and untouched by it. Matthew places her, a rescued Canaanite, directly in the family line that leads to Jesus, Matthew 1:5, and Paul describes every believer in the same terms, rescued from the wrath to come, 1 Thessalonians 1:10, waiting inside a shelter appointed beforehand rather than escaping judgment by personal merit. The type is not exact, since Rahab is spared physical death in a single battle while believers are spared the final judgment on the whole world, but the shape, marked, sheltered, and drawn out before wrath falls, is the same.

typology.type: Jericho as firstfruits devoted wholly to the LORD, Joshua 6:19
typology.fulfillment: As the very first city taken in the land, Jericho belongs entirely to God the way the first and best of a harvest belongs to the one who grew it, nothing of its plunder kept back for personal use. Paul calls Christ the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, the first installment of a resurrection harvest still to come, 1 Corinthians 15:20, and James says God brought His own people forth by the word of truth so that we would be a kind of firstfruits of His creatures, James 1:18. Jericho's firstfruits status pictures something that belongs wholly to God because it is first; the fulfillment is a people, and finally a whole new creation, given entirely back to Him for the same reason.

typology.type: Jericho tightly shut up, opened by the word of the LORD, Joshua 6:1-2
typology.fulfillment: A city sealed as completely as a gate and a wall could seal it yields the moment the LORD declares I have delivered it into your hand, before a single stone moves. The same pattern marks the tomb of Lazarus, sealed by a stone, opened at Jesus' word, Lazarus, come out, John 11:43, and the tomb of Jesus Himself, sealed and guarded, yet found open on the third day, Matthew 28:2-6. What no human strength can unseal gives way the moment God speaks; Jericho's fallen wall is a small, early rehearsal of the greater sealed places that could not hold against His voice.

study.christ:
Hebrews draws a line from this very man to a greater rest still to come: for if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, Hebrews 4:8-9. The conquest under Joshua secured land, food, and safety, real gifts, but Hebrews insists it was not the final rest, because centuries later David could still speak of today as a day to respond to God's voice, a text Hebrews quotes just before this argument. Jericho's fall is a genuine down payment on God's promise, and also a signpost pointing beyond itself, since even the man who shares his name with Jesus could not deliver a rest that lasts.

The silence of the six days matters here too. Israel does everything but fight for nearly a week, obedient and unarmed in the face of a hostile, sealed city, trusting a word that has not yet been proven true by sight. That posture anticipates Holy Saturday, the day between the cross and the empty tomb, when nothing visible had changed yet and the only thing left to do was trust the word already given. Jericho's silence breaks into a shout on the seventh day; the silence of the tomb breaks into resurrection on the third.

Most directly, the chapter sets judgment and mercy side by side and lets them meet in a single moment: the city falls under the ban while Rahab, marked by a cord and a promise, is drawn out alive. That is the shape of the gospel in miniature. At the cross the judgment sin deserves fell in full, and everyone who has taken shelter in Christ, like Rahab sheltering behind a promised sign in her window, is drawn out alive from a judgment that justly consumed everything else. Rahab is not merely rescued and forgotten; Matthew places her by name in the line that leads to Jesus, Matthew 1:5, so that the very gospel she foreshadows also, in the end, includes her.
study.god:
The same event that judges also discriminates with total precision. Everyone inside Jericho's walls falls under the ban except one household, and the dividing line is not nationality, since Rahab is a Canaanite by birth, but whether someone has taken hold of the LORD's word. That she keeps living among Israel to this day, verse 25, means the text is not describing a temporary mercy but a settled inclusion; God's judgment on Canaan's sin never once falls on the person who turns from it in faith, however unlikely that person's background.

His faithfulness extends even to a warning. Centuries after Joshua speaks the curse over anyone who rebuilds Jericho, the historian of Kings records that Hiel of Bethel laid its foundation at the cost of his firstborn and set up its gates at the cost of his youngest, exactly according to the word the LORD had spoken through Joshua, 1 Kings 16:34. God is as faithful to a spoken curse as He is to a spoken blessing; the same book that later celebrates that not one of all the LORD's good promises had failed, everything was fulfilled, Joshua 21:45, shows here that His hard words hold with the same certainty as His good ones.

His holiness sets a boundary around what belongs to Him alone. The silver, gold, bronze, and iron of Jericho are not simply the spoils of the first victory; they are declared holy and placed in His treasury, a claim of ownership that will be violated within a chapter and will cost a man his life. God's holiness is never a private attribute kept at a comfortable distance; it reaches directly into which coins and cloaks a soldier is permitted to pick up off the ground.

And He gives before He is thanked. The promise, I have delivered Jericho into your hand, verse 2, comes before a single soldier has marched a single circuit, so the six days of silence are not Israel earning a victory but Israel walking out a gift already given. Every step of obedience that follows is simply the shape gratitude takes when the outcome has already been settled by God's own word.

crossReferences.note: By faith the walls of Jericho fell after Israel marched around them for seven days, and by faith Rahab was not destroyed with those who refused to believe, since she had welcomed the spies in peace. The two verses name the whole chapter's theology before doctrine catches up to it: judgment and rescue alike hang on faith rather than performance.

God tells Abraham his descendants will return to this land only after four generations, because the iniquity of the Amorites has not yet reached its full measure. Jericho's fall four centuries later shows that patience finally exhausted; the ban was a long deferred judgment God had announced since Abraham's own day, not an impulsive act of conquest.

Moses warns Israel in advance not to credit its coming victories to its own righteousness; the land is given because of the wickedness of the nations and because the LORD keeps His oath to the patriarchs. Jericho is the first proof of that warning in action, a city that falls to divine judgment rather than to Israelite merit.

Paul insists believers wage war though they live in the flesh, using weapons that are not of the flesh but carry divine power to demolish strongholds and every proud thought raised against God. Jericho's fall by marching and shouting rather than by siege engines is the Old Testament rehearsal of exactly this principle.

Centuries later Hiel of Bethel rebuilds Jericho and loses two sons doing it, exactly as Joshua's oath foretold. The fulfillment, recorded almost in passing, quietly certifies that every word spoken over this chapter, blessing and curse alike, was the LORD's own word and not empty rhetoric.

The spies swear our lives for your lives in exchange for Rahab's kindness, promising to spare her whole family when the LORD gives them the land. Chapter 6 simply keeps that earlier oath, so the sparing of Rahab's household is not improvised mercy but a promise made good exactly as sworn.

Hebrews argues that if Joshua had given Israel true rest, God would not have spoken later of another day, so there remains a Sabbath rest for God's people still to come. Jericho's fall secures real rest in the land, yet even that victory points beyond itself to a greater rest only Jesus, who shares Joshua's name, can finally give.

Matthew's genealogy of Jesus names Rahab as the mother of Boaz, folding the rescued prostitute of Jericho directly into the family line of the Messiah. The judgment that fell on her city becomes, for her personally, the doorway into the very story that produces the Savior of the world.

James asks whether Rahab the prostitute was not justified by her deeds when she hid the messengers and sent them out another way, pairing her in the same breath with Abraham as proof that living faith always shows itself in action. Her hiding of the spies in chapter 2 is exactly the deed James has in view.

Jesus calls Lazarus out of a tomb sealed by a stone, and the dead man walks out at a word he could not have obeyed if that word carried no power. Jericho's gates, sealed as completely as any tomb, answer the same kind of word, opening not because anyone forced them but because God had already spoken.

study.oneStory:
The promise that brought Israel this far reaches back past Egypt to a word given to Abraham: your descendants will be strangers in a land not their own, enslaved and mistreated four hundred years, but afterward they will depart with many possessions, and in the fourth generation they will return here, for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete, Genesis 15:13-16. Jericho's fall is that long promise finally landing. What looked, for four centuries, like delay was patience, giving the very nations who now fall under judgment every chance to repent that a Rahab did in fact take, while the rest of her city did not.

The conquest narrative that begins here will run for chapters yet, city after city, but Jericho sets the pattern each one follows: the land is a gift received by trust, not a prize won by strength, and every subsequent battle report simply proves the same principle again. It is also the first place the whole community learns, at cost, that what God calls holy cannot be casually handled, a lesson chapter 7 will teach again in blood when Achan forgets it.

The rescue of Rahab reaches forward much further than the conquest itself. She is drawn out of a doomed city and settled among God's people, and centuries later Matthew places her by name in the ancestry of Jesus, so the very line that produces the Messiah runs directly through a Canaanite saved on the day her city was destroyed. Revelation closes the story this chapter begins in miniature: a new Jerusalem whose gates will never be shut, because there will be no night there, Revelation 21:25, unlike a Jericho that could be sealed shut against every enemy yet still could not withstand the LORD's own word. What fell at Jericho by a shout, evil entrenched and sealed against God, falls at the very end of the story for good, and what was rescued there, a believing outsider drawn into God's own family, becomes the pattern for everyone gathered at last into a city that has no gates left to shut.

quiz.q: What was God's battle plan for taking Jericho?

options.text: To march around the city behind the ark for seven days and shout on the seventh, so the wall would fall by God's power.
options.note: Verses 3 to 5 give the strange, unwarlike plan that made the victory unmistakably God's.

options.text: To lay a long siege until the city ran out of food.
options.note: The city was shut up, but God's plan was not a siege; it was the marching, the horns, and the shout.

options.text: To build ramps and storm the walls with ladders.
options.note: There was no assault on the walls; God brought them down Himself after the march and shout.

options.text: To negotiate the city's surrender through Rahab.
options.note: There was no negotiated surrender; the wall fell and the city was taken, only Rahab's household spared.

quiz.q: When did the wall of Jericho collapse?

options.text: After the seven days of marching, when the people gave a great shout at Joshua's command.
options.note: Verse 20 records the wall falling after the appointed shout of faith on the seventh day.

options.text: On the first day, as soon as the priests blew the horns.
options.note: The horns sounded daily, but the wall fell only on the seventh day after the shout, not the first.

options.text: When Joshua's soldiers battered it with rams.
options.note: No battering ram was used; the wall collapsed by God's power after the shout.

options.text: During an earthquake unrelated to Israel's actions.
options.note: The text ties the fall directly to God's promise and the obedient shout, not to a chance event.

quiz.q: What happened to the silver, gold, and metal articles of Jericho?

options.text: They were declared holy to the LORD and put into His treasury.
options.note: Verses 19 and 24 set the metals apart as holy, belonging to God, not to individuals.

options.text: They were divided as plunder among the soldiers.
options.note: Ordinary plunder came in later battles, but Jericho's firstfruits were wholly devoted to God, not shared out.

options.text: They were left in the ruins untouched.
options.note: They were not left behind; they were gathered into the LORD's treasury as holy things.

options.text: They were given to Rahab as a reward.
options.note: Rahab's household was spared and settled, but the metals went into the LORD's treasury, not to her.

quiz.q: Who was spared when Jericho fell, and why?

options.text: Rahab and her household, because she had believed and hidden the spies.
options.note: Verses 22 to 25 record her rescue in fulfillment of the oath, grounded in her faith.

options.text: The king of Jericho, who surrendered at the last moment.
options.note: The king did not surrender or survive; it was Rahab and her family who were spared.

options.text: All the women and children of the city.
options.note: The city came under the ban; only Rahab's household was spared, not all the women and children.

options.text: No one; the entire city was destroyed.
options.note: Rahab and all with her in her house were saved, so not everyone perished.

quiz.q: What does the fall of Jericho teach about how the land was won?

options.text: It was the LORD's gift, taken by faith and obedience, not by Israel's military might.
options.note: The strange strategy and the pre-given promise make the victory God's, received by faith, Hebrews 11:30.

options.text: It was won by superior Israelite tactics and weapons.
options.note: The whole point of the strategy was to exclude human might; the victory was God's, received by faith.

options.text: It proved that God helps only the strongest armies.
options.note: The opposite: God brought the wall down by His power, not because Israel was the strongest.

options.text: It showed that the outcome was really just luck.
options.note: The text credits the LORD, who promised the city and gave it; nothing here is chance.

questions: God had Israel win by marching and shouting rather than by fighting, so no one could boast. Where are you tempted to trust your own strength or strategy instead of trusting God's way?
The people had to stay silent and obedient for six long days before the victory came. How do you handle the waiting when God calls you to keep trusting before you see any results?
Judgment fell on the guilty city while believing Rahab was rescued. How does the fall of Jericho help you hold together both the seriousness of God's judgment and the wideness of His mercy?
Jericho's firstfruits belonged wholly to God, and grasping them would be sacrilege. Is there anything that belongs to God that you are tempted to treat as your own?
Hebrews says the walls fell by faith. Where do you need to raise a shout of faith at God's word, trusting the victory to Him before you can see it?

translationNotes.note: Devoted to the LORD for destruction renders a form of the Hebrew cherem; the BSB footnote explains it as giving persons or things over to the LORD, by destroying or offering them, also in verses 18 and 21.
The wall will collapse renders a phrase the BSB footnote also gives as fall under itself or fall flat; the same expression recurs in verse 20.
Verse 26 is poetic in the BSB; the poem lines have been joined in order as running text. The BSB footnote points to 1 Kings 16:34, where the curse is fulfilled.
